before the Unfailing King Avalokiteśvara,
those who burn this King of Incenses and recite it [shall attain their aims].
All mental intentions and all wholesome dharmas shall be fully accomplished.
*Amoghapāśakalparāja Sūtra*, Scroll Seventeen; *Amoghapāśakalparāja Sūtra*, Scroll Eighteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.

Chapter Thirty-one: The Mantras of the Ten Stages. Regarding the Mantra of the Single Syllable: [The mantra is as follows: *Oṃ vajratīkṣṇa-duḥkhaccheda-prajñājñāna-mūlāya svāhā.* Chapter Thirty-one: The Mantras of the Ten Stages.
The Mantra of the Single Syllable is as stated above.
Oṃ. Raise the voice from the throat and draw out this syllable; the same tone applies to the preceding and following syllables.
Recite this mantra with a mind of great compassion, contemplating Avalokiteśvara, and maintain it according to the Dharma.
One should skillfully practice ten kinds of superior activities. What are these ten?
First, taking non-apprehension as the means.
One cultivates the supreme mental action of purity;
that is, with a mind characterized by the wisdom that knows all things to be non-empty,
one cultivates and accumulates the activities of the supreme mental action consisting of all roots of goodness.
Because they are unattainable. Second, taking non-attainment as the means,
one cultivates the karma of a mind of equality toward all sentient beings.
That is to say, by means of the mind of wisdom that realizes all things are not empty,
one brings forth the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy,
and equanimity, because all sentient beings are unapprehendable.
Third, one cultivates the practice of giving by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means; that is,
by means of a mind characterized by the wisdom that knows all things to be non-empty.
One practices giving without making any conceptual distinctions regarding any sentient beings, because the giver,
the recipient, and the gift itself are all unapprehendable.
Fourth, taking non-apprehension as the skillful means,
one cultivates the practice of associating with virtuous friends;
that is, seeing how all virtuous friends guide and transform sentient beings.
One should cause them to cultivate the mind of the wisdom of all non-empty wisdoms;
one should then draw near to them, honoring, respecting, praising, and extolling them,
inquiring after and receiving the true Dharma, and serving them without weariness.
Because there is no dualistic distinction between virtuous friends and evil friends;
fifth, one cultivates the activity of seeking the Dharma by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means.
That is to say, with a mind characterized by the wisdom that knows all things to be non-empty,
one diligently seeks the unsurpassed true Dharma of the Tathāgata,
without falling into the stage of the śrāvaka or the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
Because all dharmas sought cannot be apprehended,
sixth, one takes non-apprehension as the skillful means to cultivate the practice of perpetual renunciation.
This means that in all places of birth, they constantly feel weary of the household life as a noisy and cluttered prison;
they always delight in the pure renunciation of the Buddha-dharma without anything being able to obstruct them,
because the home they have abandoned can no longer be found.
Seventh, by taking non-apprehension as the means,
one cultivates the practice of loving the Buddha’s body;
that is to say, having seen even a single image of the Buddha for a moment.
Until they attain unsurpassed bodhi,
they never abandon the mental attention of mindfulness of the Buddha,
because the primary marks and secondary signs are ultimately unapprehendable.
Eighth, taking non-apprehension as the skillful means,
one cultivates the activity of expounding the Dharma teachings;
that is to say, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, and so forth.
He expounded parables, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, and *upadeśa*.
Whether while the Tathāgata was in the world or after his parinirvāṇa,
he revealed and elucidated the Dharma teachings for the sake of all sentient beings.
It is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; its words and meaning are skillful;
it is a pure, singular, complete, and pristine holy life, because the phenomena that are analytically distinguished cannot be apprehended.
Ninth, taking non-apprehension as the skillful means,
one cultivates the practice of destroying arrogance;
that is, constantly maintaining humility and respect to subdue the mind of pride.
Because of this, one is not born into low castes or base lineages,
as all phenomena of worldly prosperity cannot be apprehended.
Tenth, one employs non-apprehension as the means.
One cultivates the karma of constant truthful speech;
that is, speaking in accordance with what one knows and acting in conformity with one's words,
because the intrinsic nature of all speech is unapprehendable.
One who thus cultivates this mantra will be able to destroy all evil and heavy offenses of the past and present;
all defilements and obstacles will be completely extinguished.
Then all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, dragons, and spirits will be filled with joy;
and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, together with all those who have realized their vows, will grant their blessings.
Upon the end of this life, one shall go to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, where one will dwell in the Lotus-Born state of the Stage of Supreme Joy.
The two-syllable mantra is as follows: [Oṃ Hrīḥ].
Oṃ ekākṣara. Recite this mantra with a heart of great compassion, contemplating Avalokiteśvara.
Receive and maintain it according to the Dharma, contemplating and practicing until the eight dharmas are perfected.
What are the eight? First,
the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*),
which means not giving rise to the mental orientations of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor any other forms of broken discipline.
First, because it obstructs bodhi;
second, knowing gratitude and repaying kindness,
meaning that even a small favor received is not forgotten nor left unrewarded.
How much more so for great kindness, which one ought not to fail to repay.
Third is abiding in the power of patience;
that is to say, even if sentient beings come to assault and destroy one, [one remains patient].
Furthermore, one harbors no mind of malice or harm toward them.
Fourth is the reception of supreme joy,
which means that once the sentient beings to be converted have attained maturity.
The body and mind are at ease and one experiences supreme joy.
Fifth is not abandoning sentient beings;
that is, the mind of rescuing and delivering sentient beings never ceases.
Sixth is the constant arousal of great compassion,
which means forming this thought:
"I act for the benefit of all sentient beings."
Suppose each were to remain in the great hells for as many immeasurable and innumerable *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* eons as there are sands in the Ganges, undergoing all manner of intense sufferings—
whether being burned, boiled, hacked, or severed.
Whether by piercing, hanging, grinding, or pounding,
they undergo such immeasurable sufferings until they are caused to mount the Buddha-vehicle and attain parinirvāṇa.
Even when the entire realm of sentient beings has been exhausted in this way,
his great compassionate heart never grows weary.
Seventh, he possesses reverent faith toward all teachers and elders.
Receiving instructions and making offerings with the thought that they are serving a Buddha—
meaning, seeking unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—
one should be reverent and compliant toward teachers and elders, having no regard for anything else.
Eighth is the diligent pursuit and cultivation of the dharma-pāramitā.
This means that regarding all the dharma-pāramitās,
one studies and practices them with single-minded devotion, remaining far removed from all other activities.
One who practices this mantra in such a manner can destroy the obstacles of the immediate (ānantarya) karmic offenses of the past and present;
all various kinds of illnesses will be completely extinguished.
No ghosts or spirits shall cause untimely affliction or distress.
The deity Maṇibhadra and the deity Vaiśravaṇa shall guard and maintain their wealth and treasures, providing constant protection.
Amitābha Buddha will appear to bear witness.
When life has been relinquished,
one shall be reborn within the precious palace of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva on Mount Potalaka.
Abiding in the Ground Free from Defilement,
one attains the siddhi of the mantra of the Heart-King Dhāraṇī of the Unfailing Lasso,
which then manifests before oneself.
The three-syllable mantra is:
Oṃ Padme Hūṃ. One should thus receive and uphold this mantra of Great Compassion, which contemplates Avalokiteśvara, according to the Dharma.
One dwells in the cultivation of five dharmas. What are these five?
First, one diligently seeks out extensive learning without ever becoming weary, yet does not cling to the literal words of the teachings heard.
That is to say, one arouses diligent effort and forms this thought:
"Whatever True Dharma has been taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, whether in this Buddha-field or in the worlds of the ten directions."
I shall listen to, study, recite, and uphold them all,
yet remain unattached to the words therein.
Second, with an undefiled mind, one should constantly practice the gift of Dharma.
Although he extensively transforms and guides others, he does not exalt himself;
he proclaims the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings,
yet he does not even regard these roots of goodness as his own, dedicating them toward enlightenment.
How much more so for seeking other matters?
Though he extensively transforms and guides others, he does not rely on this as a basis for self-conceit.
Third, he plants various roots of goodness to adorn and purify the Buddha-land.
Although he employs dedication, he does not exalt himself;
that is, he practices various roots of goodness with courageous diligence,
desiring to adorn the pure lands of all Buddhas.
And fourth, for the sake of purifying the mental lands of oneself and others;
although one acts for these purposes, one does not become self-exalting.
Fourth, for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Although he does not grow weary of the boundless cycle of birth and death,
he does not exalt himself,
desiring instead to bring all sentient beings to spiritual maturity.
They plant all roots of goodness and adorn and purify Buddha-fields;
even until they have perfected the knowledge of all modes,
they undergo the arduous sufferings of boundless birth and death.
Fifth, although they abide in a sense of shame and remorse, they remain unattached,
meaning they single-mindedly seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Because he possesses a sense of shame and dread of blame, he never for a moment gives rise to mental orientations toward the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas,
yet he remains unattached even to those [orientations].
For one who cultivates this mantra in such a manner,
the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara will appear before them in the form of a youth and grant blessings for all their aspirations.

One attains the vision of the supreme Lotus-Crested Maṇḍala, the mantras, maṇḍalas, mudrās, and samayas of all the great lotuses, as well as the secret mantras, maṇḍalas, mudrās, and samayas of all the Tathāgatas.
When life has been relinquished,
one will be reborn in a pure land and abide on the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).
The four-character mantra is as follows:
Oṃ bhaṭṭāra-hrīḥ. One who holds this mantra according to the ritual should contemplate the Great Compassionate Heart Avalokiteśvara.
One should abide in ten dharmas and constantly practice them without abandoning them. What are these ten?
First, one should abide in *āraṇya* (forest hermitages) and never depart from it.
That is to say, seeking unexcelled, perfect,
and complete enlightenment and transcending the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
one therefore never abandons the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka).
Second, they abide in fewness of desires;
they do not even seek great enlightenment for themselves,
much less worldly gain, fame, or similar matters.
Third, abiding in contentment:
because one is single-mindedly intent on realizing the wisdom of all non-empty gnosis,
one is without attachment to other matters and remains content.
Fourth, they never abandon the virtues of the Tathāgata and always engage in analytical reflection upon the profound Dharma.
Fifth, they never forsake any of the training rules.
Fifth, they remain firm and unshakable in the precepts they have studied,
yet do not grasp at signs within them. Sixth,
they develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward all sensual pleasures.
One does not give rise to thoughts of desire regarding sublime sensual pleasures.
Seventh, one is constantly able to arouse a mind associated with tranquility, meaning one realizes that all phenomena have never been produced through volitional effort.
Eighth, one relinquishes all possessions.
Regarding internal and external phenomena, they have never grasped at anything.
Ninth, their minds do not stagnate or sink;
they never give rise to thoughts regarding the stations of consciousness.
Tenth, one should have no attachment or longing for anything whatsoever;
that is, one should not engage in mental deliberation regarding any phenomena.
One who cultivates this mantra in such a manner [attains success].
All supramundane activities will be swiftly accomplished.
The Tathāgata Akṣobhya will manifest his body, place his hand upon your head, and declare:
"You have now attained a body of pure karma, and all hindrances and obstructions have been extinguished."
Upon being born in my land, one shall realize the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*),
avoid birth from a womb, and abide on the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arcismatī-bhūmi*).
The five-syllable mantra is as follows:
Oṃ bhaṭṭāraka-mahā-sabhu-ni. Recite this mantra with a mind of great compassion, contemplating Avalokiteśvara, and maintain it according to the Dharma.
One should distance oneself from ten things. What are these ten?
First, one should distance oneself from household life.
That is to say, their disposition is such that they desire to travel to all buddha-fields;
wherever they are born, they always delight in leaving the household life,
shaving off their hair and beard, and taking up the alms bowl.
Wearing the three dharma-robes and appearing as a śramaṇa,
he should maintain two points of distance from all bhikṣuṇīs;
that is to say, he should always remain at a distance from all bhikṣuṇīs.
One should not dwell with them even for the duration of a finger-snap,
nor should one give rise to any contrary thoughts toward them;
thirdly, one should distance oneself from the stinginess regarding one's home.
That is to say, one reflects thus:
"I should, throughout the long night, bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings;
yet now, this sentient being acts according to the power of their own merit."
Since I have been able to obtain such an excellent family of donors,
I ought not to harbor stinginess or envy toward them.
Fourth, one should distance oneself from anger and strife within assemblies.
That is to say, one reflects thus:
"If within this assembly there are śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas,
or if the essential teachings corresponding to their respective vehicles are being expounded."
"This would cause me to fall away from the mind of great enlightenment (mahābodhicitta). Therefore, I must certainly distance myself from the assembly.
He further thought:
Those who harbor anger and contention cause sentient beings to give rise to hatred and malice,
thereby committing various kinds of evil and unwholesome karma;
this already contradicts the path to the happy realms, let alone the attainment of Great Enlightenment.
Therefore, one must certainly distance oneself from anger and contention.
Fifth, one should distance oneself from self-praise and disparaging others;
that is, one perceives nothing whatsoever regarding internal or external phenomena.
Therefore, one should distance oneself from praising oneself and disparaging others.
Sixth, one should distance oneself from the ten unwholesome paths of action;
that is, one should reflect: "These ten evil dharmas even obstruct rebirth in the happy realms."
How much more so for great enlightenment;
therefore, one should remain far removed from it.
Seventh, one should remain far removed from the arrogance of overweening pride.
That is to say, one does not perceive any phenomenon that can give rise to arrogance.
Eighth, one should distance oneself from perversions;
that is to say, one observes that the objects of perversion are entirely unfindable.
Ninth, one should distance oneself from hesitation;
that is, observing that the objects of hesitation are entirely unfindable.
Tenth, one should distance oneself from the karma of greed, hatred, and delusion.
That is to say, one does not perceive at all the phenomena of greed, hatred, or delusion.
One who cultivates this mantra in such a manner destroys all outflows and obstructions,
attaining fearlessness regarding the body and fearlessness regarding the Dharma.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāpadma appeared before him and addressed him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have amassed a great mass of merit and roots of virtue for awakening through this Great King Amoghapāśa Padmottara Dhāraṇī-mantra maṇḍala, mudrās, and samaya."
They shall all attain maturity.
After your life comes to an end,
you shall make offerings to ninety-two hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta Ganges-sands of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Having cultivated and matured their roots of goodness,
they come to my land,
born by transformation within lotuses and dwelling on the stage of "Extremely Difficult to Conquer."
The six-syllable mantra is:
Oṃ bhaṭṭārakāya avalokiteśvara. This mantra is the Great Compassionate Heart-Mantra for contemplating Avalokiteśvara.
One should receive and uphold this according to the Dharma.
One should practice six dharmas. What are these six?
First, one should bring to perfection the pāramitā of generosity and the pāramitā of ethical discipline.
The perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence,
the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom—
these are said to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Abiding in these six pāramitās,
the Buddhas and those abiding in the two vehicles are able to cross over to the shore of all that can be known in the past.
The shore of what is known in the present;
the shore of what is known in the future;
the shore of what is known as unconditioned.
The shore of the ocean of the knowable is unspeakable.
Second, one should distance oneself from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
speaking as follows:
The minds of the śrāvakas do not realize the path to unsurpassed great bodhi;
therefore, they should be avoided.
Furthermore, it is said that the minds of pratyekabuddhas certainly cannot attain the wisdom of all non-empty knowledge.
Therefore, one should distance oneself from it.
Third, one should distance oneself from a mind of feverish affliction, which is to say:
making such statements as these.
The mind that fears the heat and affliction of birth and death does not realize the path to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; therefore,
one should distance oneself from it.
Fourth, when a beggar comes, his mind feels no weariness or distress;
he reflects: "This mind of weariness and distress is not the path capable of realizing great enlightenment."
Therefore, one remains definitively detached.
Fifth, one relinquishes all possessions with a mind free from sorrow or regret;
that is to say, one forms this thought regarding such a mind of sorrow and regret: [it is unwholesome].
Because it would certainly constitute an obstacle to the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I abandon it.
Sixth, I never deceive those who come seeking [my help].
That is to say, one should reflect:
"This deceitful mind is certainly not the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Because when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva first resolves upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhicitta*),"
He made this vow:
"Whatever I possess that is given to those who come seeking it,
may it not be in vain according to their desires."
How could one now deceive them?
One who practices this mantra in such a manner shall transcend the five obstacles and realize the accomplishment of the Secret Heart Mantra of the Lotus Crown.
One beholds the palace gates of all the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings opening;
one achieves mastery over both mundane and supramundane dharmas;
and one encounters all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions.
A great radiance was emitted, illuminating and touching his body.
At that moment, as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm simultaneously manifested their forms, observing and comforting him.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Padmakuṭadhvaja appeared before him and spoke words of consolation:
"The practices you have cultivated shall all be accomplished;
you shall be born in my land and abide on the stage of Presence."
Until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, the seven-syllable mantra is as follows:
Oṃ padma-hasta jvala hūṃ tiche. This mantra is the Great Compassionate Heart-Mantra of Avalokiteśvara.
One who upholds [this teaching] in accordance with the Dharma should remain far removed from twenty things.
What are these twenty?
First, one should completely distance oneself from the grasping at a self, the grasping at a sentient being,
the grasping at a life-force, the grasping at a living soul,
the grasping at a nourisher, and the grasping at a person.
The grasping at a person, the grasping at a living being,
the grasping at a soul, the grasping at a youth, the grasping at a knower,
and the grasping at a seer— namely, viewing [the self] as a sentient being, and so forth, up to a knower and a seer.
Because they are ultimately unobtainable.
Second, one should distance oneself from the attachment to annihilationism;
that is, one contemplates that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen.
Because it has the sense of being non-interrupted,
one should abandon the third type of eternalism,
namely, by contemplating the impermanent nature of all phenomena.
Fourth, one should distance oneself from the perception of signs,
because one observes that the nature of affliction is unapprehendable.
Fifth, one should distance oneself from the attachment to views such as those concerning causes.
This means that one does not perceive the intrinsic nature of any views whatsoever.
Sixth, one should distance oneself from attachment to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);
this means observing that the intrinsic nature of name-and-form is entirely unapprehendable.
Seventh, one should distance oneself from attachment to the aggregates (*skandha*),
which means contemplating that the nature of the five aggregates is entirely unapprehendable.
Eighth, one should distance oneself from attachment to the sense bases (*āyatana*).
This means observing that the nature of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) is entirely unapprehendable.
One should distance oneself from attachment to the elements (*dhātu*),
meaning one observes that the nature of the eighteen elements is entirely unapprehendable.
Tenth, one should distance oneself from clinging to the truths,
meaning that one contemplates how the nature of all truths is ultimately unapprehendable.
Eleventh, one should distance oneself from clinging to dependent origination.
This means observing that the nature of all dependent origination is entirely unapprehendable.
One should dwell having distanced oneself from the twelvefold attachment to grasping within the three realms;
this means observing that the nature of the three fruits is entirely unapprehendable.
Thirteenth, one should distance oneself from all attachment to phenomena (*dharma*),
meaning that one should contemplate how the nature of all phenomena is like space and is entirely ungraspable.
Fourteenth, one should distance oneself from attachment to all phenomena as being either conformable or non-conformable to reality.
This means observing that the nature of all phenomena is entirely unapprehendable;
there is no such thing as a nature that conforms to reality or one that does not conform to reality.
Fifteenth, one should distance oneself from the clinging to views based on the Buddha.
This means that because one relies on attachment to views regarding the Buddha,
one cannot perceive the Buddha; therefore,
one should distance oneself from attachment to views regarding the Dharma.
This means that because the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is realized as being invisible.
Seventeenth, one should distance oneself from the attachment to views regarding the Saṃgha;
this means knowing that the harmonious assembly is signless (*animitta*), unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and invisible.
Eighteenth, one should distance oneself from attachment to views based on the precepts,
because one knows that the natures of both transgression and merit are neither existent nor non-existent.
Nineteenth, one should distance oneself from fear of the dharma of emptiness.
That is to say, one contemplates that all empty phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
and that the objects of fear are ultimately non-existent.
Twenty [points] should be abandoned as they contradict emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This means observing that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.
Since emptiness does not contradict emptiness,
one should further fulfill twenty kinds of dharmas.
What are the twenty?
First, one should fully realize and penetrate emptiness;
that is, realizing that the specific characteristics of all phenomena are empty.
Second, one should fulfill the realization of the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*),
which means not conceptualizing any signs whatsoever.
Third, one should fulfill the knowledge of dwelling in the wishless (*apraṇihita-vihāra*).
That is to say, the mind dwells nowhere amidst the phenomena of the three realms.
Fourth, one should fulfill the purity of the three wheels;
that is to say, being fully endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action and the purity of the three wheels.
Fifth, one should fulfill compassion for sentient beings;
that is to say, having already attained great compassion and purified the buddha-field,
one fulfills compassion for sentient beings and remains without attachment toward them.
Sixth, one should fulfill the view of the equality of all phenomena;
that is, regarding all phenomena, one neither adds to nor subtracts from them, remaining without any attachment.
Seventh, one should fulfill the view of the equality of all sentient beings.
That is to say, regarding all sentient beings, there is neither increase nor decrease, neither grasping nor abiding. Eighth,
one should fulfill the thorough penetration of the principle of reality,
namely, the principle of reality regarding all phenomena.
Although he truly penetrates [reality], there is nothing to be penetrated; he is without grasping and without abiding.

Ninth, he should fulfill the wisdom of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which means enduring that all phenomena are without arising, without cessation, and without volitional construction.
Furthermore, knowing that name and form are ultimately unarisen,
one should fulfill the tenth [perfection] by teaching the principle of the single characteristic of all phenomena;
that is, practicing the non-dual characteristic regarding all phenomena.
Eleventh, one should fulfill the complete eradication of conceptualization,
which means not giving rise to conceptualization regarding any phenomena.
Twelfth, one should fulfill the complete distancing from all perceptions.
That is to say, one should fulfill the thirteen ways of distancing oneself from all notions of smallness, greatness, and the immeasurable; specifically,
one should distance oneself from all views of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth.
Fourteenth, one should fulfill the complete distancing from afflictions;
that is, the relinquishing of the continuity of all outflowing (*āsrava*) afflictions and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Fifteenth, one should fulfill the stages of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
This refers to cultivating the samaya-wisdom of the non-empty path-wisdom of all things.
One should fully perfect the sixteen [aspects] to subdue the nature of the mind;
that is, one should neither delight in nor be moved by the phenomena of the three realms.
Seventeenth, one should fulfill the nature of a tranquil mind;
that is, the nature of a tranquil mind through the proper restraint of the six sense faculties.
Eighteenth, one should fulfill the nature of unimpeded wisdom.
That is to say, one cultivates and attains the nature of unimpeded wisdom of the Buddha-eye.
Nineteenth, one should fulfill the state of being free from all attachment,
which means being able to skillfully relinquish the six external sense bases.

The twentieth perfection consists in being able to travel to all Buddha-fields at will according to one's heart's desire and manifesting one's own body within the assemblies of Buddhas; that is to say,
the cultivation of supreme supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
They travel from one buddha-field to another,
making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and praising the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
they entreat them to turn the wheel of Dharma for the benefit of all beings.
For one who thus cultivates this mantra,
all things will be perfected, free from defilement and fear;
they shall attain the lotus-like samādhi of purity and freedom from hindrances.
From his body issued forth a multitude of lights that universally illuminated the trichiliocosm;
wherever these lights reached within all the palaces,
they manifested clouds of oceans of light-flower blossoms made of various jewels.
He made offerings to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Then the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Padmaprabha manifested his body,
placed his hand upon [his] head, and addressed him, saying:
Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
That which you practice is the most secret heart-essence offering method of all Tathāgatas;
it is also the samaya of the Great Lotus-Crown Maṇḍala of the true, secret, and firm heart of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
You have now attained the perfect accomplishment of the supernatural powers of King Amogha-padma-śekhara;
you shall be born in my land, abide on the Ground of Far-reaching Progress (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi), and perform great Buddha-work.
The eight-syllable mantra is:
Oṃ āḥ muḥ ga ma ṇi padme. This mantra is the Great Compassionate Heart-Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara.
One who maintains [the teachings] according to the Dharma should fulfill four qualities. What are these four?
First, one should fully master the entry into the mental activities of all sentient beings.
That is to say, by means of the wisdom of the non-empty single mind,
one thoroughly knows, as they truly are, the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings;
second, one should fulfill the mastery of all supernormal powers.
That is to say, sporting with various sovereign supernormal powers,
they travel from one buddha-field to another for the sake of beholding the Buddhas.
Furthermore, one should not give rise to the thought of wandering through Buddha-fields.
Third, one should fulfill the vision of all Buddha-fields and,
according to what is seen, personally adorn and purify various Buddha-fields.
This means that while dwelling in a single buddha-field, one is able to see the boundless buddha-fields of the ten directions and can also manifest them,
yet never gives rise to the conceptual mark of "buddha-fields."
Furthermore, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity,
he manifests and dwells in the position of a universal monarch (cakravartin) over a trichiliocosm, adorning himself with its splendors;
yet he is able to renounce it all without any attachment.
Fourth, one should perfectly fulfill the offerings and services rendered to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
observing the body of the Tathāgata as it truly is,
for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
They correctly discern the meaning and intent of the Dharma,
serve the Buddhas with the offering of the Dharma,
and furthermore, they contemplate the Dharma-body of all Buddhas with clear insight.
For one who thus cultivates this mantra,
their body becomes perfectly pure like a crystal gem.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva appears before them, touches their head, and says:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
Having now attained the mind of concentration for supreme bodhi,
you shall follow me to the pure land of the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja."
Abiding in the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), one extensively performs Buddha-activities.
One attains the siddhi of the King of Non-Emptiness (Amogharāja) and the Lotus-Crested Mandala-Seal, which is the most supreme dharma of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
The nine-syllable mantra is as follows:
Oṃ bhaṭṭāraka-māralocana hūṃ phaṭ. This mantra is the Great Compassionate Heart-Mantra for contemplating Avalokiteśvara.
One should receive and uphold this according to the Dharma.
There are four dharmas that should be fulfilled. What are these four?
First, one should fulfill the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings.
That is to say, abiding in the ten powers of a Buddha,
one knows as they truly are the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings;
second, one should fulfill the complete purification of the Buddha-field.
That is to say, by employing the method of non-apprehension,
one purifies the mental activities of all sentient beings;
third, one should fulfill the samādhi of illusion-like concentration and enter various meditative absorptions repeatedly.
This means that while abiding in this samādhi,
one can accomplish all activities yet the mind remains unmoved,
because the cultivation of samādhi has reached full maturity.
Without applying deliberate effort, these four qualities manifest repeatedly.
Fourth, in order to bring the roots of virtue of all sentient beings to maturity as appropriate,
one enters into various states of existence, manifesting through spontaneous birth.
That is to say, in order to bring to maturity the sublime roots of goodness in all classes of sentient beings,
one enters into various states of existence and manifests birth according to what is appropriate for them;
such is the cultivation and refinement of this mantra-practitioner.
Having received the prophecy, he was named Avalokiteśvara-putra. Then,
hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges,
simultaneously manifested before him through various supernatural powers.
Reaching out his hand to stroke the crown of [his] head, he spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
This mantra-sūtra which you have practiced and cultivated..."
All supramundane and mundane dharmas shall be accomplished.
Upon casting off this life, one will be reborn in my land and proceed to the Stage of Good Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
The ten-syllable mantra is as follows:
Oṃ bhaṭṭākarasiṃhasamaye hūṃ phaṭ. This mantra is the Great Compassionate Heart-mantra for contemplating Avalokiteśvara.
One who upholds [the Dharma] according to the Dharma should fulfill twelve kinds of dharmas.
What are these twelve?
First, one should fulfill the gathering of all great vows regarding infinite locations.
May all their aspirations be fulfilled,
because they have already fully cultivated and perfected the six pāramitās;
or may it be for the purpose of adorning and purifying the buddha-fields.
Or, for the sake of maturing all classes of sentient beings,
they cause whatever their hearts desire to be fully accomplished. Second,
they should perfect the knowledge of the various languages of different species, such as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
That is to say, for the sake of cultivating the supreme analytical knowledge of language,
one thoroughly understands the distinctions among the vocal expressions of sentient beings;
third, one should fulfill the unimpeded wisdom of eloquence.
That is to say, for the sake of cultivating the supreme analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) so as to be able to teach inexhaustibly for the benefit of all sentient beings,
one should fulfill the four requirements for a perfect descent into the womb (*garbhāvakrānti*).
This means that although he is in fact always born by transformation in all places of birth,
for the benefit of sentient beings he manifests entry into a womb,
wherein he is fully endowed with various kinds of supreme qualities.
Fifth, he should be fully endowed with a perfect birth;
that is to say, at the time of emerging from the womb, he manifests various rare and sublime events,
causing all sentient beings who see them to rejoice and attain great peace and happiness.
Sixth, one should fulfill the perfection of family lineage;
that is, being born into a great kṣatriya clan or born into a great brāhmaṇa clan.
7) One’s lineage should be perfect and complete,
meaning that one is always born into the lineage of the great bodhisattvas of the past. 8) One’s retinue should be perfect and complete.
That is to say, he has as his retinue exclusively immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattvas,
and not various other classes of beings;
ninth, he should be perfected in the full endowment of the birth-body (*janmakāya*).
That is to say, at the moment of birth,
his body was fully endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence,
and he emitted a great radiance that shone throughout boundless Buddha-worlds.
He also causes that realm to undergo six kinds of transformations;
any sentient beings who encounter them will all receive benefit.
Tenth, he should fulfill the perfection of renouncing the household life.

That is to say, at the time of his renunciation, he was followed and escorted by immeasurable and innumerable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
He proceeded to the place of enlightenment, shaved off his hair and beard,
donned the three dharma robes, and took up the alms bowl,
leading forth immeasurable numbers of sentient beings.
He causes them to mount the three vehicles and proceed toward parinirvāṇa.
Eleventh, he should be fully endowed with the complete adornment of the Bodhi tree;
that is to say, through his supreme roots of goodness and the power of his vast vows.
He brought forth such a wondrous Bodhi tree:
its trunk was made of deep blue lapis lazuli jewels,
and its roots were formed of genuine vajra-jewels.
With the most exquisite seven precious jewels as its branches and leaves, it bore various flowers and fruits;
the tree was so high and broad that it completely covered the trichiliocosm,
and its radiance shone forth, pervading Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
Twelfth, one should fulfill all merits through their complete accomplishment and perfection;
that is to say, fulfilling all the provisions of sublime merit and wisdom,
maturing sentient beings, and purifying the Buddha-fields.
In this way, for one who fully cultivates and masters each of these mantras,
all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the infinite *koṭi-nayuta* lands throughout the ten directions— equal in number to the sands of the Ganges— will [appear].
Manifesting various supernatural powers all at once, he proclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You shall constantly serve as a refuge for all devas, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and the eight classes of beings, as well as for the people of the world."
Setting aside immeasurable reverence,
one who attains this Lotus-Crested Mantra-Vidyādhara shall [proceed] until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Abiding on the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*),
he performs Buddha-activities in accordance with the needs of those to be converted in every direction.
Guhyapati, you have asked about the practice of this *dhāraṇī-mantra*.
Each and every one can accomplish the supreme siddhi.
This is the samaya of the mantra of the Heart-King Dhāraṇī of Amoghapāśa;
I shall now expound the superior, middling, and inferior rites.
Those who thus read, recite, receive,
and uphold this [text] should always bathe and purify themselves, anoint their bodies with incense,
wear clean garments, and give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.
Speak words of truth, have deep faith in the Triple Gem, and respectfully serve and make offerings to one's preceptors, teachers, parents, and virtuous friends;
fully maintain the vows and uphold this Dharma.
One who thus undertakes the practice is called a person who truly upholds the mantra;
such a person will certainly and decisively attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets, [spoke].
Upon hearing this teaching, he rejoiced with a smile;
rising from his seat with palms joined like a revolving wheel and holding a ritual mace,
he bowed deeply and said with palms pressed together, "O Noble One!"
These mantra-samayas are collectively named the *Amogharāja-padmaśekhara-guhyahṛdaya-maṇḍala-vistara-dhāraṇī-mantra-samaya*.
Regarding these dharani mantras,
anyone who merely reads, recites, receives,
and upholds them shall all achieve accomplishment and perform great buddha-work.
If one performs a great offering according to the Dharma,
one should, at the appropriate time each month, abstain from speech and food for one day and one night,
subsisting either solely on fruit or by consuming only milk.
Furthermore, if one constantly consumes the three white foods and diligently recites,
chants, and upholds [the teachings] day and night,
what merit will such a person obtain and what roots of goodness will they accomplish?
"In which land do they dwell, and what Dharma-gates do they bestow?
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets, saying:
Thus, this is collectively named the Samaya-mantra of the Amogharāja-padma-śekhara-dhāraṇī.
Secret Lord, listen, listen attentively!
Whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, or laywomen—
On the first day of the waxing moon, one should perform service and offerings,
remain silent, abstain from all speech, and consume the three white foods;
then, recite, chant, and uphold the mantra of the Padmaśekhara Dhāraṇī.
First, contemplate each individual syllable as being like a garland of sunlight.
Second, contemplate the light of the syllables manifesting Avalokiteśvara.
Third, contemplate the light of the syllables manifesting the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Fourth, he entered the samādhi of the pure dharma-realm through the sovereign power of the intrinsic nature of the light of syllables.
From it flowed forth various gates of supernormal powers and samādhis,
continuing without interruption day and night for eight days.
If one observes the fast by abstaining from food for one day and one night,
this person shall attain the eradication of the suffering of five ānantarya crimes that would otherwise require an eon in the Avīci hell.
Upon the end of his life, he will be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss,
born by transformation from a lotus flower and endowed with the knowledge of past lives;
his merit, lifespan, and longevity shall endure for eighty thousand kalpas.
They shall experience supreme bliss,
and in every successive birth, they shall never again fall into the three evil realms.
Furthermore, they shall attain rebirth in the world of Ābhāsvara.
For sixty-two thousand kalpas he experienced supreme happiness;
furthermore, he was reborn as Lokāloka,
where for seventy-two thousand kalpas he enjoyed great bliss.
Furthermore, they will be reborn in the world-realm of Ratnavijaya,
where for twelve thousand kalpas they shall become great Vidyādhara mantra-sages of the Great Jewel-holders.
Thereafter, they will be reborn within the precious palace of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva on Mount Potalaka.
For eighteen thousand kalpas, they will experience the bliss of all dharmas;
furthermore, they will be reborn in the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
where for ninety thousand kalpas they will enjoy celestial happiness.
Furthermore, they will be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven,
where they will enjoy celestial bliss for eighty thousand kalpas;
thereafter, they will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
For hundreds of thousands of great kalpas, he served as Śakra, Lord of Devas, enjoying great bliss;
furthermore, he was reborn in the lands of the ten directions,
where for fifty thousand kalpas he sported with supernatural powers.
He traveled through various Buddha-fields to make offerings to the Buddhas and experienced all manner of bliss;
furthermore, for twenty thousand kalpas, he acted as a great mantra-vidyādhara.
Until they reach enlightenment, they shall never again undergo birth from a womb, an egg, moisture, or transformation.
In whatever place they are born, they will always attain miraculous birth and possess the knowledge of past lives.
O Lord of Mysteries, having served and made offerings for seven days and seven nights, they shall read, recite, and uphold [this teaching].
If one can attain such a vast accumulation of merit and endowment with roots of goodness as this,
how much more so for those who are able to eat the "three white foods" every first day of the waxing moon?
Recite, chant, receive, and uphold this Lotus-Crown Dharani mantra without ceasing day or night.
On the eighth day of the waxing moon, abstain from food for both day and night.
Ceasing all speech, recite and uphold [this mantra] in accordance with the Dharma.
Will it not manifest before one's very eyes and grant realization of the Great Amogha-vighna-viśuddhi-samādhi and the Amogha-alaṃkāra-samādhi?
The Samādhi of the Radiant Flames of the Miraculous Transformation of the Unfailing Lotus;
the Samādhi of the Unfailing Pure Light;
the Samādhi of the Unfailing Contemplation of the Banner.
This is the *Amoghapadma-vimala-darśana-samādhi* (The Samādhi of the Vision of the Stainless Lotus of Non-Emptiness).
Is it not the *Amoghapadma-mūrdha-jvālā-guhya-hṛdaya-samādhi* (The Samādhi of the Secret Heart of the Blazing Radiance on the Crown of the Lotus of Non-Emptiness)?
Furthermore, this person shall serve ninety-two koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Having ripened the roots of goodness,
upon the cessation of life, one shall go to the Land of Peace and Bliss.
There, one will be born miraculously upon a lotus pedestal and attain the Samaya of the Seal of the Liberation Altar of the Unfailing King Lotus-Crest.
And they all manifested before them as Vidyādharas of the vast and non-empty mantras.
Chapter Thirty-Two: Worldly Accomplishments. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Guhyakādhipati Vajrapāṇi...
Again, he addressed him, saying: "O Greatly Compassionate Holy One,
for the sake of fulfilling the aspirations of all sentient beings,
please deign to demonstrate this Lotus-Crown Dhāraṇī mantra maṇḍala and the method for the accomplishment of the mantra."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, saying:
"If there should be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, sons of noble family, or daughters of noble family..."
One should serve, make offerings to, revere, and prostrate according to the instructions of the samādhi;
constantly arouse great compassion toward all sentient beings;
and every day, recite and maintain the mantra of the Root Lotus-Crested Dhāraṇī in accordance with the Dharma.
First, contemplate each individual syllable as being like a garland of sunlight.
Second, contemplate the light of the syllables manifesting Avalokiteśvara.
Third, contemplate the light of the syllables manifesting the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Fourth, one contemplates the light of the syllables to accord with and penetrate all profound and inconceivable natures of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
which are equal to space and unimpeded in their own characteristics—
the mind of perfect awakening regarding the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Emitting inexhaustible sounds with a pure mind free from self,
recite this twenty-one times;
it will certainly cleanse away all heavy karmic offenses of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.
One shall attain great roots of goodness and achieve a vast accumulation of merit.
One will not be harmed by any worldly poisons, venomous insects, calamities, monsters, diseases, afflictions, or the harassment of malevolent spirits.
For this reason, one should employ this dhāraṇī mantra.
Consecrate clean sand twenty-one times with mantras and scatter it over corpses in a śmaśāna,
or scatter it upon graves and tombs; wherever such things are seen, scatter it there.
Those deceased who were undergoing various intense sufferings in their respective realms shall all attain liberation and be reborn in the heavens.
This may be done by using paper, silk, bamboo, or cloth.
Having transcribed this *Mūla-padma-kuṭa-dhāraṇī-mantra* and other such mantras,
place them atop a stūpa or upon a banner.
All beings with two feet, four feet, many feet, or no feet—
All sentient beings— whether born from a womb, an egg, moisture, or by transformation—
whoever has their body reflected in the shadow of a stūpa,
or who sees it or touches it.
All shall attain the eradication of every karmic obstruction and,
upon casting off this body, will be reborn equally in the heavens.
If one consecrates a conch shell and blows it with great force from a high vantage point, [the same result follows].
Sentient beings of the four modes of birth who hear the sound of the conch shell extinguish all grave offenses;
having cast off their received bodies, they are reborn equally in the heavens.
If there are good sons or good daughters who have previously received the Bodhisattva precepts—
whether the two hundred and fifty precepts, the five hundred precepts, the five precepts, the ten precepts, the eight precepts, or the three refuges—
Those who hear the sound of the conch shall, after casting off this body,
go directly to the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the west to be born by transformation within a lotus flower and dwell on the stage of non-retrogression.
If one consecrates white sandalwood incense and burns it within a city or town, [the same benefit shall accrue].
May all sentient beings who smell this fragrance have their various karmic obstructions completely eliminated.
If one burns this incense or perfumes their body and clothing with it, [the same shall occur].
One will also be able to eliminate the defilements and obstacles of envy;
one will be seen by others with joy and receive their respectful salutations.
If one perfumes the body or clothes, or wears it as a sacred thread according to the ritual, [the same benefits shall be obtained].
Facing the sun, recite the Lotus-Crown Dhāraṇī mantra once.
To "call upon the Sun God" once means that the Sun God will provide protection.
If one consecrates agallochum and white sandalwood incense before Maheśvara, recites the Padmaśekhara Dhāraṇī mantra once,
and calls out "Maheśvara" once while burning it;
Maheśvara shall act as a protector to fulfill all wishes.
If one recites this mantra before Nārāyaṇa once for each incense offering to Nārāyaṇa, [the same result shall be attained].
The deity Nārāyaṇa shall provide protection and fulfill all wishes.
If one consecrates white mustard seeds and white sandalwood incense before Mahābrahmā,
reciting this single mantra once for each offering, and burns them before Mahābrahmā...
That Great Brahmā shall provide protection and fulfill all wishes.
If one empowers dry lotus powder and white sandalwood incense before Mahākāla with this single mantra as follows:
First, regarding the invocation of Mahākāla the Burner:
the deity Mahākāla shall act as a protector and follower when entering mountain forests to extract hidden treasures.
All medicinal herbs will be obtained according to one's wish.
If one consecrates dragon-flower white sandalwood incense with this mantra, [it shall be effective] by the side of a dragon pool. Thus is the mantra.
Having once called the name of the dragon and burned [the offerings],
he then recites the mantra while holding white mustard seeds and scatters them into the water of the pool while rapidly chanting the mantra.
The retinue of the Dragon King shall all provide protection and act according to the will of the mantra-practitioner.
If one performs empowerment within a śmaśāna (cremation ground) by burning human charcoal mixed with white sandalwood incense, [the desired result will be achieved].
If one recites and maintains this mantra while making a great roar within a śītavana charnel ground and performing the fire ritual,
all yakṣas and spirits will manifest their own forms.
One may perform various life-sustaining rites until the end of one's lifespan.
Alternatively, if one joins two *guṇḍarī* leaves together and fumigates them with blended charcoal incense according to the ritual rules, [the same result is achieved].
If one empowers a *guphara* with mantras,
one will immediately gain mastery over spirits and ghosts for all matters of life.
If one prepares the ground to construct a mandala, [the same result follows].
Smear it with cow dung as a ritual coating.
Upon the center of the maṇḍala, draw two yakṣiṇīs in vermilion.
Sprinkle unhusked rice grains as a boundary around the four sides of the maṇḍala.
Offer parched non-glutinous rice within the mandala.
Use the aforementioned charcoal incense;
thus, for each recitation of the mantra, call upon the yakṣiṇī and burn the offering.
Furthermore, by reciting one mantra for each white mustard seed while striking the image of the yakṣiṇī,
the true yakṣiṇī will appear before you and come forth;
she will then serve as a messenger at your command, acting according to the will of the mantra-practitioner.
If one requests her to act as a mother,
she will constantly follow and protect them as if guarding an infant,
providing all necessary wealth and treasures.
If one requests her to become a sister,
she will provide clothing and money daily without any lack.
If one consecrates agallochum incense and white sandalwood incense [with mantras], [the desired result will follow].
Pressing the head of Puṇyavatī with one’s hand,
if one recites this mantra once for each invocation of Puṇyavatī while burning [incense],
one shall obtain Puṇyavatī as a protector who provides guardianship.
One will obtain great wealth and abundance from all manner of treasures.
Likewise, if one recites this mantra once before King Vaiśravaṇa while burning [incense], [the result shall be attained].
The deity Vaiśravaṇa bestows one thousand taels of gold.
Before the deity Maṇibhadra, for each such mantra recited,
one should offer a maṇi-bhadra incense stick as an oblation.
The deity Maṇibhadra will come and give one thousand gold coins.
Furthermore, in great mountains or forests,
if one recites this mantra once and calls upon it, the medicinal essence will be incinerated.
All medicinal essences will appear for one to gather at will.
If one recites a mantra once at each of the four gates of a city and burns [the substances] once,
all calamities and obstacles within the city will be immediately eliminated.
If one recites the mantra once and burns [the incense] once in every place where there is danger from tigers, wolves, and the like,
those dangers of tigers, wolves, and so forth will be immediately eliminated.
If there is an illness caused by spirits or ghosts, one should recite the mantra once before the patient and burn [the incense] once to fumigate the patient.
One will immediately obtain the eradication of diseases caused by ghosts, spirits, and the like.
This Lotus-Crested Gāthā Medicine possesses the great supernatural power of the King of the Present Clan;
it is empowered by Īśvara, Śakra Devendra, Maheśvara, and Mahābrahmā.
May the god Viṣṇu and the Four Heavenly Kings grant their grace, protection, and respectful praise.
Take equal quantities of high-quality camphor, aloeswood, ox-gall, cloves, and sandalwood, grind them together,
and mix them with the ichor from the ears of a white elephant to form pills.
Place it within the mandala before Avalokiteśvara, and empower that medicine with the Lotus-Crested Dhāraṇī,
the Family-mantra of the Wrathful One, and so forth, until the three signs appear to Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets.
Purify the body and clothing.
Grind medicinal substances into a paste and apply dots on the forehead, the crown of the head, the upper arms, the chest, and both elbows.
Wear one pellet on each arm and hold one pellet in the mouth.
Entering among the great assembly, he will be loved and respected by others,
possessing a majesty and accumulation of merit like our own.
Whatever words he speaks to discipline sentient beings, they will all be subdued and compliant.
If they enter the monastic community, they will be cherished by the Sangha;
they will be looked upon and praised just as we are,
fulfilling the various aspirations of all sentient beings.
All celestial beings, rishis, nāgas, and the eight classes of spirits will reverently protect them.
No poisons, venomous insects, sorcery, curses, ghosts, or spirits shall cause them any harm or disease.
Furthermore, they shall not be subjected to unjust flogging or imprisonment by kings or their ministers, nor shall they suffer various afflictions;
nor shall they be harmed by any evil yakṣas, rākṣasas, lions, tigers, wolves, thieves, bandits, thunderbolts, enemies, or other such calamities.
Furthermore, he wears medicinal pills upon his head and likewise smears medicine all over the wheel;
carrying the wheel, he enters the midst of another's military array.
Those who see his troops will naturally be reconciled.
If one enters a royal city, all people whom they encounter will pay him respect with joy.
If one suffers from a demonic illness that cannot be cured by treatment, [he shall be healed].
Have him take this medicine;
furthermore, if he bathes with this medicine mixed with warm water, he will be cured.
If he suffers from sores or swellings, [he shall likewise be healed].
By mixing the medicine with water and grinding it to apply over the sores and swellings, all shall be healed and cured.
Because of this, all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas will no longer cause him harm or affliction.
If one uses the medicine according to the Dharma,
all Buddhas and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva will bestow their grace and protection, causing one's roots of goodness to increase.
One will experience great peace and happiness in this life and future lives.
Wherever one is born, the Vajradhara Guhyapati and his retinue will protect and sustain one.
If one consecrates medicinal preparations with clarified butter, [the same result shall follow].
One attains great wisdom and understands all sūtras and śāstras.
Furthermore, the Lotus-Crested Gāthā Medicine— manifesting within this section as the supreme siddhi-samaya of all mantras— consists of gandhārī and tagara.
Mṛgamada-kṣīra, surabhi-nakṣīra, sugandhika-sa-phaṭika,
śamkha-kṣīra, nāga-puṣpa-keśara, utpala-puṣpa, padma-bīja-tuṣa, aguru, kuṅkuma.
White *candana* sandalwood, *śilārasa* (spikenard), along with *nyagrodha* flowers and cloves,
in quantities such as *bīru* and *pala*, should be ground according to the ritual rules, blended together,
and placed within the mandala before Avalokiteśvara. Then, using the *Padma-śekhara-dhāraṇī*...
Having empowered the medicinal herbs one hundred times with the *Kulakrodha-mantra* and other mantras,
mix them with Persian honey, camphor, and other ingredients, boiling them with water according to the ritual rules.
Form the medicinal pills with the mantra into the size of jujube fruits and place them within the mandala before Avalokiteśvara.
By means of the Padmottama-dhāraṇī, the Kula-krodha-mantra, and others such as the Amoghapāśa-rājñī-dhāraṇī, empower the medicine; it will manifest three signs.
Place it in a clean vessel and dry it in the shade. Keep the medicine pure, secret, and secure, and do not let it be defiled or touched by impure hands.
Vajrapāṇi, Lord of Secrets,
when employing medicinal substances,
one should first bathe for purification, anoint the body with incense, and put on clean garments.
Consecrate black mustard oil and mix it with the medicine;
by anointing it upon one's body, one will attain mastery at will.
One may enter the caves of asuras, nagas, and spirits, proceeding everywhere without obstruction.
These spirits and ghosts shall carry out the tasks as commanded.
If one consecrates the milk of a *saṃgha* cow and mixes it with medicine, applying it to the forehead and the heart;
He then reflects upon the various obstacles and burdens of superior, middling, and inferior persons, contemplating their removal.
If he consecrates fragrant oil mixed with medicinal herbs, [he should do so].
If one anoints both shins and the palms of both hands,
one will walk as swiftly as the wind, traveling twice the usual distance in a day, and treading upon water without becoming wet.
If the medicine is mixed with human milk and applied to both eyes, [the same results follow].
He immediately attained the ability to travel at will to various villages,
roaming and observing with sovereign ease, being loved and respected by others; or,
in the presence of people, he could move objects simply by thinking of them in his mind.
It causes all people to be unaware [of its presence].
If one applies it to the face, the body, or the hands,
and enters among the great assembly to perform various hymns of praise, [the effect is as described].
He caused the people to observe and praise only his voice, not his body.
Then, having filled a jar inside and out with pure water,
he carried it into the midst of the assembly and poured the water from it while holding it high.
At that time, the people observed only the water beneath and did not observe the image of the jar.
If one coats the interior and exterior of a basin and fills it completely with pure water,
then the multitude of people will observe only the water and not the image of the basin.
If one consecrates fragrant oil with medicinal herbs and applies it to the body or uses it to fumigate one's robes,
then upon entering the caves of asuras, nāgas, or yakṣas,
one will attain mastery over them all, such that they cannot cause mutual harm or disturbance.
If one enters beneath the water, the water cannot drown them;
the sentient beings within the water likewise do not harm them.
If one enters into fire, the fire cannot burn them.
If one enters a dragon pool, the dragon cannot cause harm.
Regarding all the various worldly matters and dharmas,
whatever one intends and recollects in the mind will be accomplished.
If one constantly and diligently upholds this dharma,
day by day one will increasingly perceive the various phenomena of the world, both sentient and non-sentient, through the power of mindfulness.
Furthermore, the *padmottara-siddhi* medicine is able to manifest various miraculous transformations.
They shall attain great peace and happiness and abound in wealth and treasures; at that time,
the people of the world will compete to offer worship with lotus filaments and pollen, *kācavā*, *gandharasa*, incense, ox-gallstone (*gorocanā*),
bamboo-resin (*khaḍgarasa*), realgar, saffron, blue *utpala* flowers, and sea-foam.
Small *agallochum*, sandalwood, yellow *āmalaka*, and others, equal in number and prepared with refined ingredients according to the ritual;
furthermore, *kakkola* incense together with musk, Persian honey, and so forth,
are blended and placed within the mandala before Avalokiteśvara, using the Padma-śekhara Dhāraṇī.
The Family Wrath Mantras and others empower the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja), who manifests three signs;
Vajradhara, the Lord of Secrets,
cleanses the body and robes with water mixed with medicinal herbs ground together.
Having smeared it all over one's limbs, hands, feet, head,
and face, and having applied it to the eyes,
one immediately realizes mastery in the secret samādhi.
If one loudly utters the syllable HŪṂ,
all ghosts and spirits will immediately behold great flames of light issuing from one's body;
one will not drown when entering water, nor will one be burned when entering fire.
Entering the midst of the great assembly, he made his request from within their hearts.
He scattered medicinal herbs into the air and invoked the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
who manifested in the forms of all the celestial and terrestrial deities.
They manifest the appearances of all sentient beings;
they manifest the various stages of the causal grounds of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
and they manifest the appearance of relinquishing their heads, eyes, marrow, brains, bodies, flesh, hands, and feet.
In mid-air, he manifested the sign of water flowing from his upper body and fire issuing from his lower body;
he manifested signs of killing, reviving, and disintegration.
Whatever was requested by the mind, it was dispersed according to that mind and immediately appeared before them all.
Furthermore, apply the medicine to one's body.
Also, empower scented oil with the medicine and apply it to the head and the palms of both hands.
Having burned and fumigated his body and adjusted his robes,
he entered among the fourfold assembly with a composed and slow gait,
and requested the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
Entering the samādhi of the contemplation of water and the samādhi of the contemplation of fire, one lies supine in mid-air.
One visualizes the body emitting water from below and fire from above,
while various sounds of celestial music issue forth.
He manifested them all accordingly.
Furthermore, he empowered the sap of the *duzhong* tree mixed with medicine and smeared it upon his body,
hands, and feet before entering the great assembly.
I take refuge in Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
who manifested in the past as a bodhisattva bestowing upon others their kingdoms, positions, wives, concubines, sons, daughters, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures;
and who sat at the site of enlightenment to subdue the hosts of Māras.
All divine transformations, flower-and-fruit palaces,
exquisite celestial garments, and various ornaments—
whatever is requested shall manifest immediately according to one's thoughts.
That is to say, so that sentient beings with wrong views and impaired wisdom may behold these supernormal powers,
give rise to the bodhicitta, and seek the Buddha-way with faith,
he preaches this Dharma.
The Amoghapāśa-kalparāja-sūtra, Scroll Eighteen; The Amoghapāśa-kalparāja-sūtra, Scroll Nineteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Four: The Accomplishment of Homa.
Furthermore, there is the homa-siddhi-samaya, which is able to extinguish all karmic obstructions, calamities, and misfortunes.
One attains great peace and happiness, eliminates all enemies and thieves,
and accomplishes the samaya of the mandala and mudrās of the Manifestation of Non-Emptiness;
one is thus able to summon all devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings.
It can subdue all vināyakas and cause all people to rejoice,
for it enables one to attain great diligence and constantly behold all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and mahāsattvas.
The Vajrapāṇi deity and all the celestial deities shall provide protection.
O Lord of Secrets, empower non-glutinous rice, white mustard seeds, agallochum, clarified butter, and honey;
then perform homa before an image of Avalokiteśvara using the secret heart-mantra.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva manifests transformation bodies to grant whatever vows are sought.
Furthermore, he empowers aloeswood, white sandalwood, lotus stalks, rice grains, white mustard seeds, ghee, honey, and curd.
Furthermore, for one who performs the homa of the secret heart-mantra,
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva will manifest his true body and bestow upon them the maṇḍala, mudrās, and samaya of all the Amogharāja mantras.
One spontaneously accomplishes and increases the mass of merit,
thereby entering the samaya of the maṇḍala of the lineage of all Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, there are the *śiṃśapā* and *nimba* woods.
One should perform *homa* with rice grains, black sesame,
white mustard seeds, salt, clarified butter, and curd, using a fire one span (*vitasti*) high that blazes fiercely,
while reciting the mantra of the Wrathful King of the Family.
Then one shall obtain the eradication of all obstacles caused by *vināyaka* spirits, demons, enemies, calamities, thieves, and weapons.
Furthermore, empower lotus petals, rice blossoms, white sandalwood incense, clarified butter, honey, and curd.
Furthermore, for one who performs the homa of the Secret Heart Mantra,
there will be an abundance of the five grains for a thousand yojanas, and all cities,
towns, villages, and their inhabitants will be protected.
There shall be no calamities such as pestilence, tigers, wolves, water, fire, or bandits.
Furthermore, take Du-zhong wood and Su-fang wood, each one span in length, and cut them straight; they shall spontaneously ignite in fire.
For one who performs the homa of consecrated white mustard seeds, nāga-flowers, rice blossoms, and honey, the host of nāgas will cause great sweet rain to fall and the crops to flourish.
If one desires to stop the rain, one should perform the homa by burning the ashes of *śiṣṭa* (stale food).
For one who performs the homa with white sandalwood incense,
calamities and torrential rains will all cease at once.
Furthermore, one should empower rice grains, flowers, white mustard seeds, and clarified butter.
One who performs the homa rite shall eliminate all calamities, hail, and thunderbolts;
furthermore, one should empower white mustard seeds and non-glutinous rice.
One who performs the homa will thereby eliminate calamities, evils, fierce winds, cold winds, and hot winds;
furthermore, one should empower rice husks, white mustard seeds, and black sesame.
If one performs *homa* for one year,
all malevolent *nāgas* will be subdued and shall not emit calamitous vapors.
Furthermore, by performing *homa* with consecrated white mustard seeds and clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one shall obtain the eradication of all diseases caused by spirits and deities.
Furthermore, if one performs homa with *dhatura* wood, *kuṭaja* leaves, salt, and rice husks while performing empowerment,
all enemies and calamities will be eliminated.
Furthermore, by consecrating lotus petals, black sesame, white mustard seeds, rice blossoms,
and clarified butter, one who performs the homa will establish a great boundary extending for a thousand yojanas in every direction.
Furthermore, if one performs homa with sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, ghee, and black mustard oil while performing empowerment,
all evil vināyakas, hosts of demons, ghosts, and spirits will be firmly bound.
Furthermore, if one performs homa with empowered hemp seeds, salt, and mustard oil,
all evil yakṣas, rākṣasas, malevolent spirits, and ghosts will be terrified and flee in all directions.
Furthermore, one should empower a *duzhong* tree and kindle a fire;
then, empowering rice grains, flowers, and clarified butter,
one performs the *homa* offering.
All pure-practicing brahmins will joyfully believe and submit.
Furthermore, one should empower rice grains, flowers, *duzhong* wood leaves, granulated sugar, and clarified butter;
those who perform the homa with these [substances] [shall attain success].
The Kṣatriya caste will joyfully provide offerings.
Furthermore, by consecrating madanaphala fruits and kaṇikāra medicine and performing homa with them,
[the desired result will be achieved].
Śuddhārā joyfully made offerings. Furthermore,
one who performs *homā* with *jvalamitra* medicine mixed with clarified butter,
empowered by mantras, [shall attain success].
All the Vaiśyas will joyfully make offerings.
Furthermore, one should empower *sumanā* flowers and perform *homa* with them.
All women will joyfully take refuge in and have faith [in him].
Furthermore, by consecrating lotus petals with clarified butter and performing *homa* with them,
[the desired result is achieved].
All young maidens will joyfully pay him homage.
Furthermore, by consecrating rice grains with clarified butter and performing a homa sacrifice with them, [one achieves this].
One shall attain the cessation of all disputes and slanderous matters.
Furthermore, by consecrating barley, wheat, rice, black beans, small beans, sesame, white grains, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*),
one who performs the *homa* offering [shall achieve this].
One shall obtain all manner of wealth, treasures, grain, and silks, which will increase of their own accord.
Furthermore, if one consecrates white mustard seeds mixed with honey and performs homa with them, [the same result follows].
One will receive the respect and praise of all people.
Furthermore, by consecrating *dhatura* flowers, white mustard seeds, *śāli* rice flowers, and clarified butter,
one who performs the *homa* offering [shall achieve success].
One shall obtain fortune and prosperity;
furthermore, it is like holding the stalk of a lotus or a water lily,
measuring one span in length.
One who performs the homa with ghee smeared on both ends shall obtain hidden treasures.
Furthermore, one should empower asafoetida, black mustard seeds, ghee, and honey.
For one who performs the homa,
all yakṣas will assemble to serve as messengers;
furthermore, one should consecrate black pepper, non-glutinous rice, ghee, and honey.
One who performs the homa facing the sun atop a high mountain peak will be protected,
watched over, and praised by the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva).
Furthermore, having consecrated black pepper, pippalī, saindhava salt, ghee, honey, and milk,
one who performs homa upon a high mountain peak while facing the moon deity [shall achieve success].
One should perform the rites of protection, visualization, recollection, and praise for the Moon Deity and the Star Deity.
Furthermore, one should empower sesame seeds, dried ginger, white mustard seeds, non-glutinous rice, ghee, honey, and curd,
and perform the homa sacrifice with them.
All the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, and non-humans shall all rejoice and provide protection for them.
Chapter Thirty-Five: The Fundamental Lotus Mandala. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara...
He addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, saying:
"This is the root mantra of the Lotus-Crown Dhāraṇī,
the samaya of the Great Liberation Lotus Maṇḍala."
It can eliminate all hindrances and obstacles for the mantra practitioner,
fulfill whatever aspirations are sought,
and lead to the realization and mastery of all dhāraṇīs and samādhi gates.
One shall attain the tenth stage, the stage of non-retrogression,
achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
sit upon the Vajra Seat, and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma.
They crush the hosts of Māras and manifest all Buddha-fields of the ten directions,
as well as the various supernatural powers of all Tathāgatas, which provide empowerment, protection, and guardianship.
It is the same as the palace and dwelling place of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva on Mount Potalaka;
it is also the site of the supreme secret great lineage maṇḍala of all Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, it is the locus for the practice and undertaking of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
it is the locus where the entire lineage of Tathāgatas attains samādhi;
and it is the locus where the entire lineage of Padmas attains samādhi.
Furthermore, it is the place where all the Vajra families attain samādhi;
furthermore, it is the place where all the Maṇi families attain samādhi;
furthermore, it is the place where all the Gandhahastin families attain samādhi.
Furthermore, it is the locus of the great mass of merit for the samaya of the Great Liberation Lotus Maṇḍala,
equal to the great ocean, Sumeru the king of mountains, and mani-jewel trees.
In accordance with the intentions and thoughts of all sentient beings,
they are all perfectly delivered and established in the ground of Bodhi;
furthermore, this is the empowerment and gathering-in of the non-empty secret Vajra.
It is the place where all roots of goodness increase;
furthermore, it is the secret treasury of all Buddha-dharmas, the treasury of Avalokiteśvara’s great compassion, the treasury of the Great Vajra, and the treasury of the Great Jewel.
Furthermore, it is the place that crushes and destroys all the uninterrupted sins of the Avīci hell for all sentient beings;
furthermore, it is the place that subdues and overcomes all devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, both human and non-human.
As for that maṇḍala, one should select an excellent site in a secluded and quiet place,
measuring thirty-two cubits, or sixteen cubits,
or twelve cubits, or again eight cubits.
He thoroughly purified the ground,
excavating away the inferior soil, tiles, stones, bones, and wood;
he filled it with clean earth, compacting it until it was level and perfectly square.
The foundation measures two and a half cubits.
It is to be thoroughly smeared and adorned with cow dung, scented water, and yellow earth.
Using cords of five-colored thread, one should measure out the boundaries of the inner and outer enclosures, both square and circular.
Upon the heart within the inner court is a thirty-two-petaled lotus flower made of the seven precious gems,
its pedestal surrounded on all sides by floral filaments.
They all struck and adhered to the terrace.
Furthermore, from each individual flower stamen,
there emerged small lotus flowers made of the seven treasures.
They are half-open, not fully blossomed;
their petals, stalks, and buds all cling closely together upon the large lotus leaves.
Upon these great lotus pedestals, there further emerge seven-jeweled lotuses in full bloom.
From atop this flower pedestal emerges Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
with one head and three faces, manifesting a golden-hued appearance,
smiling with a joyful and serene countenance.
In the center of his face, between the eyebrows, is a single eye.
He has three heads and wears a lotus-flower jeweled crown,
upon which resides an emanation Buddha.
Flames of light radiate everywhere from his hair and crown.
On the great lotus pedestals at the left and right sides of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s head,
there emerges from each a one-faced Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The upper half of the body is white-yellow in color;
on his head he wears a jeweled crown containing an emanation Buddha,
from which flames of light radiate all around his hair and throughout the crown.
